newsitem.title: zaire: Mobutu said ready to meet Zaire rebel chief at sea.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu said ready to meet Zaire rebel chief at sea.

text.p: Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko is ready to travel to Congo on Friday for talks with rebel leader Laurent Kabila aboard a South African naval ship, a presidential source said on Thursday night.

The report suggested that confusion over the timing of the meeting might have been resolved, if not wrangling over the agenda. Mediators variously announced earlier the talks would start on Friday, Saturday or Sunday.
"The president will fly to Pointe-Noire tomorrow morning and will be received by President Pascal Lissouba (of Congo). He will then be taken to the ship," the source told Reuters.

Mobutu's camp said the talks would focus on a peaceful transition with elections open to all. Kabila's side insists however the embattled president must stand down after more than three decades in power.

"The talks will just be about Mobutu and what we do with him. Our uncompromising demand is that he leaves power and we shall look after him," Kabila said before leaving his Lubumbashi headquarters for talks in neighbouring countries.
"There can be no ceasefire or indeed elections in this country until Mobutu and all he represents is removed and thrown away," Kabila added.

There was no indication Mobutu, who seized power in 1965 but is sick with cancer, was ready to step down -- although rebel "foreign minister" Bizima Karaha said the veteran president had agreed to discuss his departure.

The United States last week threw its weight behind international efforts to get the two rivals to meet to seek a peaceful end to the conflict in the vast central African country and prevent war reaching the capital Kinshasa.
U.S. envoy Bill Richardson, who helped persuade Mobutu and Kabila to meet, told reporters in Kinshasa on Wednesday there were no preconditions for the talks.
He arrived in Luanda on Thursday to discuss the Zaire crisis with Angolan leaders, and perhaps South African Deputy President Thabo Mbeki who was also due to meet Kabila there.
Mandela said through a spokesman he would chair the face-to-face talks on Friday aboard a South African naval vessel in international waters off the coast of West Africa.

Kabila's rebels, who took up arms in October, say they expect to capture the capital over the next 10 to 15 days. They now control over a half of Zaire's territory -- including all its main cities outside the capital.

Their advance was continuing on Thursday. Residents of Kenge, just 200 km (125 miles) from Kinshasa, said Mobutu's army had retreated and the town was calm and waiting for the rebels to arrive -- a familiar pattern in a seven-month campaign.
Residents of Kikwit, the rebels' forward base for their march on Kinshasa, said an expected rebel airlift into the town had not begun but reinforcements had been arriving by truck.

The war has trapped Hutu refugees, who fled Rwanda fearing reprisals after the 1994 genocide of Tutsis. Critics accuse Zaire's Tutsi-dominated rebels of killing refugees -- or at least leaving them to die.

International efforts to repatriate the Hutus gathered pace. A U.N. refugee agency official said 1,512 were flown out of Zaire's third city of Kisangani on seven flights on Thursday to Rwanda's capital or its southern town of Cyangugu.
Thousands of other Hutus, many with appalling injuries, streamed back to camps south of Kisangani as U.N. agencies struggled to clear a backlog of those waiting to be airlifted.
Aid workers at Biaro camp, 41 km (25 miles) south of Kisangani, said they could not keep up with a flood of refugees returning to camps they fled in terror after attacks last week.
In Kinshasa, some feared that if Mobutu's forces decided to make a last stand, their final card could be a "night of the long knives" in which diehard soldiers wreaked havoc.
"We are not concerned whether Kabila comes in with force or not. It is Mobutu's people and all those who have stolen with him who have something to fear," one resident said.
Kabila, after meeting Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe in Harare, was quoted by the Zimbabwean state news agency as saying he retained the option of war.
"Why not? I think we must go forward. We must liberate Kinshasa but we are now discussing with others to try and solve the problem by peaceful means," he said.
